retrieved_contexts: - Published Thousands of illegal registration plates on cars and other vehicles have been detected by a new camera system currently being tested on motorways in south-east England, BBC Panorama can reveal. These plates have been adapted to avoid their details being identified by automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) systems, which are used to enforce speed limits and low emission zones as well as to track criminals. Illegal plates are putting the public at risk and are far too easy to get hold of, according to one former government advisor. We have spoken to families who say their lives have been devastated by road deaths where illegal plates were involved. Filming undercover, we also discovered how easy and cheap it is to buy plates without any background checks. The minister responsible for vehicle registration across the UK has told us a national plan has now been instigated to understand how widespread the problem of illegal number plates is, and what can be done about it. The UK has one of the largest networks of ANPR cameras in the world, with 14,000 sites capturing 100 million number plates each day. Many experts believe this system is failing to keep up with tactics used by some drivers determined to avoid recognition. Ghost Plates: Drivers Cheating the Law How cloned and ghost number plates are leaving innocent motorists facing fines, debt collection threats and years of stress. One of the main providers of ANPR technology, MAV Systems, has been testing a new camera capable of identifying and reading ghost plates. At one test site, just outside London near the Dartford Crossing, it has recorded an average of more than 1,000 of the ghost plates a day over several months. In another case, from 2025, 81-year-old Graham Slinn was killed on a pedestrian crossing when a car with cloned plates hit him at high speed. The 20-year-old driver, Cain Byrne, who was driving without a licence or insurance, had also inhaled nitrous oxide minutes before the collision. He was identified after police trawled through hours of CCTV footage. One camera even caught the moment he had put the illegal plates on his car. Byrne was jailed for 11 years and six months for causing death by dangerous driving, driving while disqualified and driving without insurance. The victim's daughter, Nicola Timmis, says cloned plates are like a "gateway drug" which allow drivers to take more dangerous risks. "It seems like it's harmless, but then one thing leads to another, leads to another, and before you know it, it's somebody dead," she tells Panorama. "It is not a victimless crime." the naked eye. In the case of cloned ones, at least two vehicles are on the road with the same letters and numbers - with only one of them being legal. Ghost plates, on the other hand, show correct details for the vehicle - but they are made up of reflective materials which are difficult or impossible for most ANPR cameras to read. Cloned and ghost plates undermine the police's ability to track organised criminals, says Tony Porter, a former senior counter-terrorism officer who has advised the government on surveillance cameras. "The police need an effective ANPR system that doesn't have weaknesses [and] doesn't put the public at risk," he says. While passports have security features such as watermarks and electronic ID chips, Porter says, "we tolerate a £10 number plate with no security mechanism on it". In the UK, there are more than 34,000 businesses registered with the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) to supply number plates. Anyone can currently become a registered number-plate supplier by filling in a quick form and paying a one-off fee. Panorama secretly filmed at a market in Essex to find out how easy it is to buy a plate in breach of the rules. Two out of three businesses we approached there offered ghost plates which they said could help avoid cameras policing London's Ultra-Low Emission Zone (Ulez) cameras. One of them allowed us to buy a plate without asking for either ID or proof that we were allowed to use the registration - both of which are required by law. Instead, we handed over £40 in cash and, eight minutes later, we had a brand new number plate. Buying a ghost plate is not illegal in itself, but it would be against the law to put it on a vehicle and drive with it. Just two number plate suppliers have been prosecuted and forcibly removed from the DVLA register since 2020, a Freedom of Information request by Panorama has discovered. Only six DVLA officers are tasked with inspecting and auditing the thousands of registered suppliers in the UK. Not long after we arrived, officers stopped a van. Specialist infrared goggles - which see number plates the way ANPR cameras do - revealed it was displaying a ghost plate. The driver received a £100 fine but said he was unaware the plate was illegal. The police and DVLA then visited the plate supplier, where staff denied selling ghost plates. But, using the goggles to view the supplier's stock, Panorama identified two ghost plates displayed on a wall alongside several legal ones. The supplier, which told Panorama it did not manufacture the letters it used to make plates, received a warning letter, although a prosecution is still being considered. Police forces want to see tighter licensing and regulation around who can issue a number plate, says Chief Constable Tim Forber, the UK's policing lead on ANPR. "Not a week goes by where we don't see an example of someone on cloned plates involved in serious and organised crime," he adds. There is a problem that needs tackling and a more robust system may be needed, according to Justin Madders, the minister in charge of UK vehicle registration. The voluntary pact, titled the ‘White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities,’ calls on companies developing and deploying frontier AI models to establish internal controls, independent assessments and board-level oversight to manage safety risks. First, companies are expected to implement internal controls to track model capabilities and alignment during training and deployment, including cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats.
